newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong high-tech under handover spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong high-tech under handover spotlight.

text.p: Mounting controversy over Hong Kong's economic management under China surfaced on Tuesday at a showcase conference examining key business issues in the territory in the last few days under British rule.
Raymond Ch'ien Ku-fung, one of future leader Tung Chee-hwa's key policy advisers, argued forcefully in favour of the development of a high-technology industry in Hong Kong.

"We have a golden opportunity to collect Greater China's brains and combine them with capital (in Hong Kong) and create some interesting economic activities," Chi'en told delegates to the conference, organised by the Far Eastern Economic Review.
But he met opposition from David Dodwell, a prominent business commentator and author.
"There is an absolutely erroneous mantra that high-tech equals good (profits)," Dodwell said.
But figures show that, excluding Microsoft and Intel, the global high technology industry is not profitable, Dodwell said.
"And if there is one thing Hong Kong is good at, it's identifying profitable opportunities," he said.

The debate touched on an issue that has raised temperatures throughout Hong Kong's business community -- economic intervention to assist the territory's competitive edge in an increasingly tough region.

Rejecting any suggestion of government assistance for industry, Dodwell claimed he had been astonished by various ideas put forward by other members of Tung's Executive Council, or inner cabinet of appointed advisers.

These include the creation of special shares in technology companies to trade on a second board on the Hong Kong stock exchange, housing subsidies for technology company workers, a cross-border industrial zone and a Science Park, or industrial area of Hong Kong.
"How you could give preferential treatment (given Hong Kong's notorious property shortage) bamboozles me," Dodwell said.

But Ch'ien said he did not advocate government intervention in the economy. Rather than an industrial policy, Hong Kong should work to attract the best and the brightest in the region through useful education, immigration and housing policies.
"We need to be more visionary," he said.
